strengths: Well-motivated insight connecting aesthetic objectives to spatial compute allocation, with clear demonstration of aesthetics-driven spatial non-uniformity in denoising
Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation: 10,000 prompts, 30,000 images, unified implementation, multiple quality metrics, extensive ablations across three modern DiT architectures
Strong empirical results: 2.11× speedup on Lumina-Next with +11.9% ImageReward improvement, consistent gains across multiple architectures and metrics
Training-free and practical approach applicable to deployed systems without retraining; clear presentation with informative figures and detailed appendices
Thorough ablations (Figs. 4-5, Tables 7-10) clearly demonstrate complementarity of spatial and temporal components, with transparent runtime decomposition
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: individual components (spatial masking from cross-attention, step-level caching, spatial CFG) are well-established; primary contribution is their combination rather than fundamental innovation

Architecture-dependent implementation reduces generalization claims: SD3-Medium disables spatial CFG due to instability; FLUX.1-dev uses only temporal acceleration; raises questions about robustness and architectural constraints

Fixed 34-word anchor vocabulary is manually curated and covers only 65.48% of evaluation prompts; no principled justification for anchors, no comparison to data-driven or learned alternatives, and fallback behavior for uncovered prompts unexplored

Evaluation bias and limited scope: uses Pick-a-Pic dataset with high aesthetic descriptor prevalence, no human evaluation studies, only automatic metrics (ImageReward trained on same Pick-a-Pic data), generalization to non-aesthetic prompts and other datasets unknown

Temporal acceleration oversimplified: one-shot mask at step 5 assumes stable salient regions; linear extrapolation between two cached steps is crude without exploring higher-order alternatives; hyperparameter sensitivity (skip_ratio, mask_step) suggests brittleness

Incomplete code availability reference ('available at .') and unresolved architectural constraints: no clear explanation for why spatial CFG destabilizes SD3-Medium or principled guidelines for adapting to new architectures

Lack of theoretical analysis: no formal characterization of when/why spatial non-uniformity holds or how to predict applicability to new models; missing analysis of failure modes and conditions causing degradation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three DiT backbones with 10,000 prompts and multiple metrics (CLIP, ImageReward, HPS, Aesthetic, Edge), providing strong empirical validation
Thorough ablation studies (Figs. 4-5, Tables 7-10) clearly demonstrating the contribution of individual components (AesMask, spatial, temporal)
Well-executed practical system achieving meaningful speedups (1.5-2.1×) with simultaneous quality improvements on preference-oriented metrics
Extensive implementation details, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and architectural considerations enabling reproducibility and guiding future work
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (attention heatmaps, mask overlays, qualitative comparisons) and honest discussion of architecture-specific limitations
weaknesses: Limited novelty: AesMask is attention aggregation + thresholding, and SkipSparse combines well-established token sparsification with standard prediction caching. Core components (RAS, TeaCache, ∆-DiT) already explore spatial/temporal acceleration; the contribution is primarily engineering rather than scientific

Misleading 'aesthetics' framing: The mechanism fundamentally exploits attention concentration, which occurs for any important tokens regardless of aesthetic vs. semantic content. 65% trigger rate and fallback to generic masking when anchors don't match (Appendix E.3) undermines the aesthetic narrative. Critically, no human evaluation is provided to validate aesthetic quality claims

Architectural dependence weakens generalizability: SD3-Medium disables spatial CFG as 'less stable' (relegated to Appendix C.5), and FLUX uses temporal-only mode. This suggests fundamental brittleness rather than a robust general framework. The paper claims broad applicability but requires model-specific engineering

Inconsistent improvements across models and metrics: Speedup ranges 1.5-2.1×, with benefits varying significantly. On FLUX, quality improvements are marginal. Linear extrapolation for step caching (Eq. 13) lacks theoretical justification—why should predictions follow linear trajectories?

Weak theoretical analysis: The central claim that 'aesthetics and spatio-temporal non-uniformity are coupled' (page 3) is presented as empirical finding without mechanistic explanation. Why does spatial CFG fail on SD3? Why one-shot masking at step 5 vs. adaptive masking? Many choices appear ad-hoc, and Table 10 shows step 3 achieves higher speedup

Binary masking discards information: Hard percentile thresholding (Eq. 7) ignores fine-grained importance gradations; soft masking unexplored. Global keys/values in Eq. 9 still requires O(|I_t|×N) computation, overstating efficiency claims. Runtime decomposition (Table 11) shows temporal caching dominates (1.57× standalone), making spatial contribution secondary

Missing critical validation: No human evaluation despite aesthetic focus. Ablation reveals step-level caching alone reduces ImageReward (0.743 vs 0.752 baseline), raising concerns inadequately addressed. Anchor vocabulary manually curated without sensitivity analysis. Evaluation set trigger rate (65%) means method is inactive for diverse prompts

Limited analysis of failure modes and generalization: No exploration of scenes with diffuse attention, abstract prompts, or non-visual tasks. The one-shot masking strategy seems suboptimal given speedup-quality tradeoffs observed in hyperparameter sensitivity. Architecture dependence and component interactions (why does AesMask recover quality lost by StepCache?) lack mechanistic insight

strengths: Well-motivated observation that aesthetic-related regions show concentrated cross-attention and temporal variation, effectively validated through visualizations
Training-free approach enabling practical deployment without model retraining across existing DiT variants
Comprehensive experimental validation with 30,000 images (10K prompts × 3 seeds) across three backbones, multiple metrics, thorough baselines, and detailed ablations
Consistent improvements in both speed (1.5-2.1×) and quality, with notable gains on preference-oriented metrics (ImageReward +11.9% on Lumina-Next)
Clean methodology design: simple yet effective AesMask construction, spatial CFG modulation, SkipSparse preserving global context while updating focus tokens
Clear presentation, well-structured paper, extensive implementation details in appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Significant architecture dependence: spatial sparsification disabled on SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev relies primarily on temporal reuse; configurations differ substantially across backbones, undermining generalization claims

Aesthetic anchor vocabulary is manually curated (34 words, 6 categories); trigger rate only 44.9% on wild data, causing fallback to uniform weighting for ~35% of prompts; no adaptive/learned mechanism explored
Aesthetic quality claims rely entirely on proxy metrics (ImageReward, HPS, LAION predictor); absence of human evaluation particularly problematic given the paper's emphasis on aesthetic enhancement

Temporal reuse (StepCache) appears fragile: simple linear extrapolation with fixed interval (Δ=2); Table 5 shows quality degradation from StepCache alone (0.752→0.743 ImageReward); limited analysis of failure modes

Limited algorithmic novelty: cross-attention region selection, sparse attention, and caching are established techniques; main contribution is combining with aesthetic anchors (somewhat incremental); AesMask design itself is straightforward

One-shot mask assumption (step 5, reused throughout) lacks deep validation; Table 10 shows optimal mask_step but doesn't explain why; doesn't address whether different regions matter at different denoising stages
Speed-quality trade-off analysis shallow: no Pareto curves, comparisons at single operating point, unclear which baselines win at different speedup budgets
Architecture-specific workarounds (SD3-Medium: spatial CFG disabled due to pilot tuning instability; FLUX: spatial path not attempted) suggest approach is less general than claimed

strengths: Strong empirical results: achieves 2.11× speedup on Lumina-Next while improving ImageReward by +11.9%, with consistent gains across three DiT backbones and statistically validated human preference study (p<0.001)
Well-motivated insight connecting aesthetic-driven spatial non-uniformity to computation allocation, with clear intuitive appeal and extensive cross-attention visualization evidence

Exceptional experimental rigor: comprehensive baselines, multiple complementary metrics, statistically significant human study (15 annotators, 60 pairs), thorough ablations, and robustness checks across scene types and descriptor-free prompts
Exceptional transparency: detailed hyperparameters, full 34-anchor vocabulary, backbone-specific adaptations, runtime decomposition, and extensive sensitivity analyses enabling reproducibility
Practical value: training-free method with low overhead (0.18s for AesMask construction) that improves both efficiency and quality—rare and valuable trade-off
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: combines existing techniques (CLIP similarity matching, sparse attention with global keys, linear extrapolation) primarily as engineering contribution rather than introducing new algorithms or theoretical insights

Generalization concerns from fixed aesthetic anchor vocabulary: only 44.9% coverage on full Pick-a-Pic unique set (vs. 65.48% on evaluation subset), no mechanism for domain adaptation, and unclear performance on non-English or non-aesthetic-heavy domains

Architecture-specific constraints reduce claimed generality: spatial CFG disabled for SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev doesn't support spatial SkipSparse path (temporal-only), suggesting method requires careful per-architecture tuning rather than being universally applicable

Insufficient justification for claimed spatial-temporal coupling: paper asserts they are 'coupled' but provides primarily empirical observation; lacks formal analysis of why aesthetic token attention should correlate with temporal predictability

Ad-hoc failure mitigation: acknowledged failures on diffuse-attention prompts (dense crowds, abstract art); recovery via late-mask and entropy fallbacks (92.7–95.4%) lacks principled justification, suggesting core assumptions don't universally hold

Hyperparameter sensitivity and potential dataset bias: multiple interdependent hyperparameters (mask_step, skip_ratio, refresh interval) tuned to Pick-a-Pic (which is biased toward aesthetic descriptors); unclear generalization to other prompt distributions

Limited temporal prediction sophistication: StepCache uses simple linear extrapolation without exploring more sophisticated temporal modeling; correlation of predictions across timesteps not formally analyzed
Evaluation scope limitations: single resolution (1024×1024), single GPU (RTX 5090), only recent DiT variants; generalization to other hardware and older architectures uncertain

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: aesthetic descriptors create spatially non-uniform attention patterns enabling selective computation allocation; effectively visualized and empirically demonstrated.

Comprehensive experimental validation: three DiT backbones, five strong baselines, six complementary metrics, blind human study with proper randomization, and thorough ablation studies (Figs. 4–5, Tables 8–11).
Strong practical results: 2.11× speedup on Lumina-Next with +11.9% ImageReward improvement and consistent gains across diverse scene types (+1.8% to +13.7% in Table 15).
Training-free and practical: requires no model retraining, low overhead (~0.18s), compatible with existing DiT models; addresses real deployment constraints.

Rigorous documentation and reproducibility: extensive appendices with hyperparameter sensitivity (Tables 10–11), failure mitigation strategies (Sec. E.4), and architectural implementation details (Appendix A.3–A.4).
Robust to prompt variations: maintains gains without explicit aesthetic descriptors (+3.1% IR) and across six challenging scene categories (dense crowds, landscapes, indoor clutter, abstract art).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: AesMask combines standard CLIP similarity matching, cross-attention aggregation, and percentile thresholding. SkipSparse reuses established sparse attention and CFG techniques. StepCache employs simple linear extrapolation. The contribution is primarily an engineering combination of existing methods rather than a methodological advance.

Underemphasized anchor vocabulary limitations: only 44.9% of full Pick-a-Pic corpus contains diagnostic anchor hits; descriptor-free prompts gain only +3.1% IR vs. +4.8% with descriptors (Table 14). Method's performance on out-of-distribution aesthetics and novel concepts remains unclear.

Weak theoretical foundation: the claimed coupling between aesthetic spatial non-uniformity and temporal smoothness (Sec. 3.1) is assumed but not proven. No analysis of denoising dynamics, prediction error accumulation for StepCache, or principled justification for when linear extrapolation (Eq. 13) remains valid.

Architecture-dependent design requiring per-model tuning: different configurations for Lumina-Next (full spatial+temporal), SD3-Medium (spatial without CFG+temporal), and FLUX.1-dev (temporal only). Minimal explanation for architectural constraints (e.g., why spatial CFG destabilizes SD3-Medium). Limits generalization to new DiT variants.

Evaluation methodology concerns: ImageReward is a learned reward model (not ground truth). Human study is small-scale (15 annotators, 60 pairs, 3 comparisons) with no reported inter-rater agreement. Only 67% win rate vs. dense baseline is marginal. Heavy multi-metric averaging (CLIP, IR, HPS, Aesthetic, Edge) without justified weighting.

Static mask limitations inadequately addressed: one-shot masking at step 5 is empirically chosen (Table 11), not principled. In dynamic scenes, salient regions may shift; static mask risks missing late-emerging details. Dynamic refresh shows 2.08×→1.94× speedup and 0.407→0.392 IR degradation (Table 18), attributed to 'region jitter' without deeper investigation.

Unclear component attribution: which components drive quality vs. speed gains? StepCache contributes 36.4% speedup, spatial path 30.1%, but overlap obscures individual contribution. Quality decomposition across IR, Aesthetic, and CLIP missing—uncertain whether improvements stem from selective computation or spatial CFG emphasis.

Temporal accuracy concerns with StepCache: linear extrapolation assumes smooth prediction trajectories, but noise schedules vary nonlinearly. No comparison with higher-order extrapolation or learned predictors. Minimal analysis of early-step behavior or cache refresh sensitivity (Δ=2 used uniformly without justification).

Hyperparameter sensitivity and overfitting risk: multiple parameters (skip_ratio, mask_step, top-r, cache interval, warmup, CLIP model). Table 10 shows 10% IR variation across skip_ratio values (0.8415 at 0.30 vs. 0.7643 at 0.70). Limited guidance for parameter selection on new domains; concerns about overfitting to 10k evaluation set.

Limited evaluation scope: single resolution (1024×1024), fixed step counts (28–30). Scalability to 2K/4K resolutions and aggressive distillation (e.g., 4-step models) underexplored. No evaluation on non-English prompts or cultural aesthetic variations.

strengths: Well-motivated connection between aesthetic descriptors and spatial compute allocation; intuitive insight that aesthetic tokens show higher temporal variation

Exceptionally thorough experimental validation: 30,000 images across 3 backbones with fixed seeds, multiple metrics (CLIP, IR, HPS, Aesthetic, Edge), human preference study with 15 annotators, and comprehensive ablations
Rare achievement of simultaneous speedup and quality improvement: consistent gains across preference-oriented metrics while reducing latency (2.11× speedup, IR +11.9% on Lumina-Next)
Practical and deployable: training-free method with lightweight overhead (0.18s), simple design choices (percentile thresholding, one-shot masking), and clear implementation details
Comprehensive supplementary materials with extensive robustness checks: descriptor-free prompts, 6 scene categories, failure analysis with recovery rates, sensitivity analyses on key hyperparameters
Strong presentation with informative figures, clear methodology, and well-organized exposition of the approach
Honest discussion of limitations, including architectural dependencies and reliance on reliable region estimates
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (sparse attention, caching, cross-attention analysis) rather than introducing fundamental new methods; incremental contribution for top-tier venue

Hand-crafted aesthetic anchor vocabulary lacks theoretical grounding; only 44.9% coverage on full Pick-a-Pic pool with no mechanism for adaptation or extension to out-of-distribution aesthetic descriptors

Architecture-dependent design undermines generalization: SD3-Medium requires disabling spatial CFG for stability; FLUX.1-dev doesn't support spatial SkipSparse path; different hyperparameters per backbone suggest limited scalability

Key assumptions lack rigorous quantitative validation: claim that aesthetic tokens show higher temporal variation is stated but not empirically verified; no analysis of temporal consistency metrics or extrapolation error vs. distance

Modest speedups (1.5-2.1×) with unexplored trade-offs: no Pareto frontier analysis; behavior at higher speedup targets (3-4×) unknown; fixed cache interval Δ=2 with no guidance on speed-quality trade-offs

Incomplete failure mode handling: 'entropy fallback rules' mentioned in Appendix E.4 but not clearly defined; ~5-7% residual degradation without automatic detection mechanism raises concerns about robustness
Linear extrapolation (Eq. 13) oversimplified: no justification vs. higher-order polynomials or learned predictors; assumed correlated predictions between nearby timesteps but not rigorously validated

Limited scope of applicability: method optimized specifically for aesthetic quality; generalization to other quality criteria (compositional accuracy, semantic correctness) unclear; narrowly targets aesthetics-focused models
